title: When the lights go out, how will Europeans access their money?
author: thilton.drupal
description:
When the lights go out, how will Europeans access their money? Expert comment thilton.drupal 16 November 2026

Recent outages and cyberattacks have exposed the vulnerability of digital payments. The EU and UK should use their upcoming summit to develop compatible offline digital currencies.

Across Europe, economies have become increasingly digital, bringing significant benefits to businesses and consumers. However, growing reliance on digital payment systems means that when these systems fail, people are unable to spend the money in their bank accounts.

Sometimes, this is because of technical failures. On 20 October 2026, due to an extended power outage that paralysed Google Cloud services, millions of UK residents were unable to make card payments, cash withdrawals or bank transfers.

In other cases, hostile actors have launched cyberattacks that paralyse European payment systems. Figures from September 2026 show a 61 per cent year-on-year increase in cyberattacks across Europe, many of which targeted financial services.

These risks have prompted the EU and the UK to issue fresh crisis preparedness strategies, such as the UK government’s ‘Be Ready’ campaign. A key aspect of these strategies is the advice to keep adequate cash at hand in case digital systems go down.

However, the use of cash has long been in decline: only 3 per cent of UK adults mainly use cash for their day-to-day spending. Consumers increasingly prefer the convenience of digital payments, while many businesses no longer accept cash. This raises questions about whether people will have sufficient cash available when digital payment systems fail.

This problem is compounded by the fact that ATMs also require electricity to dispense cash. As a result, during a prolonged power outage or cyberattack, millions of consumers could lose the ability to pay with their cards and phones or withdraw cash from their bank accounts. 

During the 2025 Iberian blackout that brought digital payments to a standstill, many consumers without cash could not purchase even the most basic of supplies. Tens of millions of people were affected across Spain and Portugal.

Central bank digital currencies (CBDCs) that can function offline offer a solution to this problem. While both the EU and the UK have floated the idea, they must engage in much closer collaboration on their development.

Offline digital money 

Central bank digital currencies (CBDCs) are digital versions of existing national currencies that are issued by central banks – essentially, digital cash.

Unlike cryptocurrencies such as Bitcoin, CBDCs’ value does not fluctuate independently of the national currency. And while stablecoins also aim to maintain a fixed value against existing currencies, they are typically issued by private companies rather than central banks. 

CBDCs also differ from money held in standard digital bank accounts, which commercial banks owe to their customers. Unlike these deposits, CBDC holdings would not be exposed to the risk of a commercial bank failing.

The European Central Bank (ECB) is currently developing its CBDC, the digital euro. Its aim is to preserve the role of public money in the digital economy and reduce the bloc’s dependence on non-European payment providers. Similarly, the Bank of England (BoE) is drawing up a blueprint for a potential digital pound.

A key feature of the plans for the digital euro and digital pound is the ability to make payments offline.

During an electricity outage, conventional digital payments can fail because payment terminals lose access to electricity, online transactions cannot be authorized, or the payment provider’s infrastructure stops working.

The goal of both the EU and the UK is to build CBDCs that avoid these pitfalls and reflect the operational resilience of cash, albeit in different ways.

Related work

Europe could win the battle for the future of digital money

On the EU side, consumers will be able to open a digital euro wallet, and preload funds there from their commercial bank accounts. During a power outage, say due to a cyberattack, they could make payments using their phone or a physical card through near-field communication (NFC) technology. Payments would be settled directly between the consumer’s device and the merchant’s payment terminal, without requiring internet connectivity.

The use of physical cards could prove particularly valuable during prolonged power outages, as they do not require charging, unlike smartphones. The ECB is also exploring the possibility of integrating digital euros into existing payment cards rather than requiring a dedicated digital euro card.

Meanwhile, the UK is currently prioritizing a slightly different design. Instead of settling the payment immediately, payment instructions would be recorded offline, but the actual transfer of funds would only take place once connectivity is restored. 

Offline payments are not yet crisis-proof

While efforts to develop offline CBDCs are important, several challenges remain. The EU and the UK should jointly address them.

The first issue relates to the risk of double spending – when the same units of money are used to make two or more separate payments. Normally, double spending is avoided through real-time, centralized verification of payment requests. 

However, during a power outage, payment terminals cannot send these requests to banks. While both the ECB and the BoE have explored technical solutions to tackle this risk, additional work is necessary before deployment.

Another challenge relates to operational readiness. It is unclear why European consumers would be incentivized to pre-emptively fund their offline CBDC wallets, especially if they consider a power outage to be improbable.

Furthermore, European merchants need to possess battery-powered payment terminals for offline CBDC payments. During the 2025 Iberian blackout, even battery-powered terminals became unusable as their batteries ran out.

Why the EU and UK need to work together

The EU and the UK should collaborate on offline CBDCs for several reasons.

The first is their complementary expertise. On the one hand, the EU is further ahead in the development of its CBDC, with the ECB aiming to be ready to potentially issue the digital euro in 2029. On the other, the BoE can contribute valuable insights from its experiments with different offline payment technologies, particularly regarding trade-offs between security, privacy and usability.

Second, the EU and the UK are exposed to several overlapping threats. Given that they rely on common technological infrastructure, their payment networks are highly vulnerable to shared power outages and, even worse, to coordinated digital destabilization efforts by hostile actors.

Finally, European collaboration on offline CBDCs is necessary because of economic interdependence. The EU accounts for approximately 45 per cent of UK trade. Almost 77 per cent of overseas trips by UK residents were to Europe. 

Failure to collaborate would mean that, during future outages, European cross-border trade and retail transactions might become critically impaired.

Three steps towards more resilient payments

The EU and the UK should use their forthcoming 20 November summit to advance closer alignment on offline CBDCs.

The first step should be to establish recurring, joint stress tests of payment resilience. 

The ECB and the BoE can simulate a shared 72-hour power outage, testing whether CBDCs can reliably support offline transactions. This will help European policymakers to better tackle the problem of double spending and other operational challenges before deploying CBDCs.

Connect your organization with our expertise, networks and global platform

Build a strategic relationship with Chatham House, connecting your organization with our expertise, networks and global platform to engage with critical issues and audiences.

The EU and the UK should also strive to bring their technical standards closer together. This could include the development of a prototype NFC payment terminal capable of accepting offline payments in both digital euros and digital pounds. Tests could be conducted across the Irish border, where sterling and euro payments intersect.

Lastly, they should explore the expansion of offline CBDCs to cross-border transactions involving currency conversion.

During prolonged outages, businesses may need to make new payments to foreign suppliers for essential goods. The EU and UK could test whether payment providers holding both currencies could facilitate offline exchanges, allowing buyers to pay in digital pounds or euros while suppliers receive their preferred currency.

As hybrid threats to payment systems become ever more severe, the EU and the UK need to collaborate more closely on offline CBDC standards. Otherwise, they risk being woefully unprepared when the lights go out next – with devastating consequences for their supply chains and their citizens’ ability to purchase essential goods.

title: Will the US and Iran return to war?
author: jon.wallace
description:
Will the US and Iran return to war?  Expert comment jon.wallace 9 November 2026

That is not only President Trump’s decision. Iran may also reignite the conflict, in an attempt to break the US blockade.

In recent weeks there has been considerable speculation that the US would carry out new attacks on Iran once the US midterm elections were concluded. But with the vote complete, Washington’s next move remains unclear. 

In a recent 60 minutes interview US President Donald Trump said he did not see ‘any reason’ to escalate the war. It is possible that the president chooses not to resume military operations against Iran and settles for continuing the current policy of economic strangulation. But even in that case, a return to armed conflict cannot be ruled out. Tehran is unlikely to absorb US pressure quietly while its economy further deteriorates. This is the irony of the US naval blockade of Iran. There’s evidence to suggest it has effectively hurt the regime’s finances. Iran loaded no oil onto tankers in September according to some analyses. 

But the blockade is unlikely to succeed in achieving the strategic objective of forcing the regime to make significant concessions at the bargaining table. Instead, it might push Tehran to lash out, which would take all parties back to square one in this conflict.

Stalemate

The blockade of Iranian oil exports through the Strait of Hormuz has evolved over the past few months. Washington launched the operation back in April; eased it after agreeing to the Memorandum of Understanding (MoU) with Iran in June (which allowed for the reopening of the Strait); then reinstated it on 14 July as the deal unravelled.

Want to hear more on the evolving security landscape?

Join experts and policymakers at our Security and Defence Conference for candid analysis of today’s most pressing threats.

Iran wants the blockade lifted and its conditions met before it reopens and stops its attacks in the Strait. Washington wants concessions on Iran’s nuclear programme before resuming any talks on maritime security.

It’s a stalemate. But it may not last long. The deep distrust between the two sides will make Iran doubt that US concessions will be durable enough to bring it lasting economic relief. Some in the regime will believe it is better for Iran to fight on its own terms than collapse from within as the economy is throttled. 

It will not necessarily require a new US military strike on its territory for Iran to lash out at its neighbours. In 2019, Iran responded to Trump’s economic ‘maximum pressure’ tactics with a series of attacks. In May and June of that year, it struck tankers near Fujairah and in the Gulf of Oman and shot down a US surveillance drone. 

Then on 14 September, drones and missiles hit Saudi Aramco’s Abqaiq processing facility and the Khurais oil field. The Iran-backed Houthi militia in Yemen claimed responsibility, but the US and Saudi blamed Iran. The message from Tehran was clear: We will respond to extreme economic pressure by attacking Gulf energy infrastructure. 

Defending a founding narrative

There are two main reasons why Iran responded this way to economic pressure before – and why it may do so again. 

The first is ideological. Iran isn’t just defending its shipping lanes and oil exports in this war. It is protecting its founding narrative of sacrifice and endurance. This is what Washington still doesn’t seem to get.

Since its founding, the Islamic Republic has staked its reputation on not just resisting outside pressure but also defying it. Sanctions, isolation, and military threats won’t coerce or bring down the regime: that’s the message Tehran keeps telling its constituencies and adversaries. The war with Iraq of 1980 to 1988 provides the clearest illustration of the regime’s commitment to that principle. Iran fought the war almost on its own, against an adversary backed by the US and Gulf states, and it survived. A difficult year or two as a result of a blockade is hardly comparable to what the regime endured at that time. 

The second reason is practical: Iranian defiance, unlike during the Iraq war, is now aided by outsiders. The biggest source of support is China, through its purchasing of Iranian oil. No wonder US officials have reportedly urged Beijing to play a more constructive role in ending the conflict. They understand that without China, the regime’s staying power will drastically diminish.

Tehran also knows that the Gulf states want the blockade to end. The status quo is causing them tremendous economic pain. The Iranian leadership is betting that if it holds out long enough, those with the most to lose from this economic crisis – Saudi Arabia, the UAE, Qatar, and Kuwait – will press Washington harder to find an exit. 

There are limits to Iranian resilience, of course. In 1988, after Operation Praying Mantis (a one-off US strike against Iranian naval resources ordered by President Ronald Reagan) and months of mounting losses, Iranian Supreme Leader Ayatollah Ruhollah Khomeini accepted a ceasefire with Iraq. He famously likened it to drinking poison. Yet it showed that when its survival was at stake, Iran could concede (if not surrender).

But the blockade is not the same situation at all. In 1988, there was no way Iran could have won the war. Continuing would have probably led to military collapse. 

Today Iran believes it has the upper hand. Listen to statements by Iranian officials, and it is clear they believe they have already won this contest. That’s partly true. The Iranian regime will, most likely, survive this conflict and possibly avert a new major US attack, which it would define as victory. 

But it still has to address the blockade. If history is any guide, Iran will at some point resort to violence to try to force Washington to reconsider. That, in turn, is unlikely to succeed: the US has its pride, too, and its interests. US officials are convinced that the blockade is working, so giving it up won’t be easy. If anything, Washington is doubling down by giving US Central Command the green light to establish a new task force meant to ‘prevent Iran from using ground routes to transport advanced weapons and other materials.’

There’s only one way out of this stalemate: phased diplomacy, which the two sides are apparently considering. The basic sequencing is clear: In the first phase, Washington would need to partially lift the blockade in exchange for Iran reopening the Strait and ceasing all attacks against shipping. In the second, nuclear talks could take place, including the gradual lifting of sanctions and the release of frozen Iranian funds.

The two sides are keen to end the conflict. But they appear equally determined to avoid any perceived humiliation and Israel remains an unpredictable factor. Even now, it is not clear that sense will prevail.

title: Will New Zealand’s election change its foreign policy?
author: jon.wallace
description:
Will New Zealand’s election change its foreign policy? Expert comment jon.wallace 2 November 2026

The current coalition has sought closer relations with the US and rowed back climate commitments. What would change under a coalition of the left?

On 7 November, New Zealanders go to the polls in what looks set to be a closely contested general election. As elsewhere, anxiety about the cost of living has dominated the campaign. 

International affairs tend to feature at the bottom of voter concerns. However, like many US citizens voting in this year’s midterm elections, some New Zealanders blame international events like the war in Iran for the higher costs that are their top priority. 

New Zealand’s foreign policy is therefore at stake in this election. And a change of government could substantially reshape the country’s position on key issues.

The foreign policy reset

Since 1996, New Zealanders have voted in a Mixed Member Proportional (MMP) system which normally produces a coalition government.

In 2023, New Zealand formed its first three-party coalition government under MMP. The centre-right National Party, led by Christopher Luxon, was joined by the right-libertarian Act Party and right-wing populist New Zealand First Party, led by Winston Peters. Peters took on the role of foreign minister – a role he had held twice before.

As a small, open, Pacific economy, recent New Zealand governments have generally sought balance in foreign policy. On the one hand they have nurtured the increasingly important trade relationship with China, building on a long history of openness to engagement with Beijing (China has been New Zealand’s largest trading partner since 2017).  On the other hand, governments have sought security and other partnerships with the US and other IP4 countries like Japan, Australia and South Korea. 

However, after the 2023 election the coalition announced a ‘reset’ in foreign policy, aligning New Zealand more closely with the US and Australia.

This has not meant total alignment with Washington. The coalition has supported Ukraine against Russia’s war of aggression. It has stressed the importance of free maritime movement, including in the Strait of Hormuz and the Bab al-Mandab Strait. And it has stated its support for the international justice system.

But the government has also expressed interest in joining AUKUS Pillar II – an Australia–UK–US security initiative – and deepened military cooperation with the US. It has near-doubled defence spending, while weakening engagement on humanitarian issues and climate security. 

Meanwhile, relations with China have cooled. China has shifted to making public comments on New Zealand’s foreign policy – particularly its AUKUS discussions. And in May Beijing imposed travel bans on New Zealand MPs that visited Taiwan, something that New Zealand politicians have done without consequence since 1972.

Seeking a closer relationship with Washington, the coalition has maintained a ‘softly-softly’ approach to the dramatic changes in foreign policy during the second Trump administration. Wellington’s response to US pressure on Canada, Mexico and Denmark – and the multilateral system in general – has been muted. And, though government policy is to support a Two-State Solution, the conflict in Gaza and the US-Israeli war against Iran have exposed foreign policy faultlines.

In 2025, New Zealand declined to recognize Palestinian statehood, diverging from partners like Australia, the UK, Canada and France. In March, released emails showed Prime Minister Luxon wanted to show ‘explicit public support’ for the US war against Iran.

But closer security alignment with Washington has not exempted New Zealand from a higher 12.5 per cent rate of US tariffs, leading to a 13 per cent decrease in exports to the US in the first year. And it has not shielded the country from the impact of the US–Iran war. Many New Zealanders blame these factors for increasing prices at home – as do some coalition government ministers.  

What a change in government might mean

Crucially, New Zealand’s reset was not put to voters at the last election in 2023. This time, some parties have set out some foreign policy positions in advance. 

The Labour Party pledged in 2024 not to join AUKUS Pillar II. And the party says it would recognize Palestine statehood and enforce sanctions on Israeli settlements in the occupied West Bank. 

The National Party, meanwhile, has pledged to continue to invest in defence, seek new trade relationships, and boost the medicine budget of the government’s pharmaceutical agency by cutting foreign aid outside of the Pacific. 

Climate is the area of greatest division. The coalition’s interventionist approach against climate litigators risks leaving New Zealand in breach of its climate obligations. That could threaten its trade relationship with the EU. In contrast, parties like Labour promise to prioritize compliance with climate commitments and relationships with the EU, as well as Canada and ASEAN. Labour also says it would express greater support for multilateral institutions like the World Health Organization (WHO). (Under the current coalition, New Zealand has abstained from or rejected significant global health measures).

Labour has been the most proactive about publicising foreign policy commitments in its election campaign. But a clear strategy from either of the largest parties is still lacking. The stances of smaller parties, who will serve as coalition partners, are even more opaque. 

Power favouritism increases vulnerability 

Throughout the campaign, polling has shown a finely balanced race. A small percentage of undecided voters could yet install a left-wing coalition led by the Labour Party – or maintain the status quo. 

Related work

New Zealand should rethink its pivot towards the US to retain strategic autonomy in the Indo-Pacific

Were the coalition re-elected, New Zealand’s foreign policy would likely extend the first term’s agenda. Peters would probably remain in post as foreign minister. And the relationship with China will continue to be delicate, especially following recent events. In July, Peters directed remarks at a left-wing Chinese-New Zealander in Parliament that were condemned as racist at home and prompted a formal protest by Beijing. 

The pursuit of positive US relations would also probably continue under any new government. But it will need to be refined. 

The policy is predicated on the belief that Washington is a reliable security partner in the Indo-Pacific. But US attention is fixed on the Middle East and its commitment to its alliances less sure than ever – leaving New Zealand potentially vulnerable. 

Europe and the IP4 have acknowledged the need for enhanced Pacific security engagement to compensate. But the US will still need to be involved to counter China’s influence in the region. The challenge is to engage Washington without relying exclusively on it.

Informed consent at the ballot-box

As a small economy, New Zealand is more vulnerable to shocks. Russia’s invasion of Ukraine and the war in Iran have contributed to higher inflation, trade disruption, and a weaker New Zealand dollar. 

It can help New Zealand to retain a level of strategic ambiguity in its foreign policy. But this must be balanced with the right of voters to have their say in how the country positions itself and understand the trade-offs involved. 

To ensure that voters can make informed decisions, political parties need to be clearer about their foreign policy positions. Parties should define the principles and red lines they will use to guide relations with the US and China, spell out their positions on security alliances, and more clearly articulate what they see as New Zealand’s role in the Pacific.

These positions need not be fixed or undermine strategic ambiguity. But parties should outline their policies clearly enough for voters to evaluate them. If either party believes another ‘reset’ in foreign policy is necessary, they should make an argument for it and win New Zealanders’ consent at the ballot box.

title: The war is pushing Iran closer to Russia
author: thilton.drupal
description:
The war is pushing Iran closer to Russia Expert comment thilton.drupal 2 November 2026

A flurry of diplomatic meetings and positive statements suggest Tehran sees closer cooperation with Moscow as key to its short-term survival and long-term deterrence.

The US-Israeli war with Iran is fundamentally changing how Tehran views Russia. Moscow was previously perceived by some in Tehran as an unreliable partner that benefited disproportionately from Iran’s support. But Russia is now increasingly seen as an important partner to ensure Iran’s military survival, post-war reconstruction and long-term deterrence. 

Positive meetings

In October alone, senior Iranian and Russian officials held three high-level meetings, reflecting the growing importance both governments attach to the partnership. 

On 8 October, Iran’s president Masoud Pezeshkian met Russian president Vladimir Putin in Turkmenistan on the sidelines of regional summit meetings. They emphasized the mutual political will to deepen ties across virtually every sector, including trade and economic cooperation.

On 19 October, Russia’s foreign minister Sergei Lavrov travelled to Tehran for the first since the war began on 28 February. He met President Pezeshkian, Foreign Minister Abbas Araghchi and Supreme National Security Council head Mohsen Rezaei. They discussed energy, transport and broader bilateral relations. The meetings emphasized the need to advance the comprehensive strategic partnership signed in January 2025, continuing economic and investment cooperation despite the challenges posed by the war.

Related work

Russia–Africa Summit: Moscow is engaging more with Africa, but its delivery is limited

After the meetings, Araghchi stated: ‘never in our history have Iran and Russia worked as closely as now.’ Pezeshkian thanked Russia for its support during the war. Security chief Rezaei also emphasized Tehran’s determination to strengthen strategic cooperation with Moscow, indicating that Iran’s security leadership also supports closer relations. 

On 27 October, Pezeshkian visited Moscow to attend the Gas Exporting Countries Forum, where he again held talks on bilateral cooperation with Putin. Pezeshkian thanked Putin for ‘backing and assistance’ in both political and economic matters. Putin said that bilateral trade increased by 10.4 per cent during the first eight months of 2026.

Putin also reaffirmed Moscow’s commitment to ongoing projects, including the Bushehr nuclear power plant. Russia’s state-owned nuclear corporation, Rosatom, announced it would increase the number of its construction workers at Bushehr to 200. Rosatom had evacuated its staff after the outbreak of the war. 

Outside of this nuclear development, the substance of these meetings was not significantly different to previous high-level exchanges. What stands out, however, is the increasingly positive tone of public statements by senior figures across Iran’s political and security establishment. This suggests a more favourable assessment of Russia’s strategic value, although it does not necessarily indicate a fundamental change in the views of all Iranian decisionmakers.

Moving beyond scepticism

This enthusiasm contrasts with earlier doubts within Tehran about the benefits of investing in Moscow as an ally. Elements of the Iranian leadership have long held a deep-seated scepticism towards Russia. 

This scepticism had grown since late 2022 as some in Tehran questioned the returns on its support for Russia’s war in Ukraine. Iran has supplied Russia with thousands of drones, including Shahed-131 and Shahed-136 models, along with other military assistance. Iran has publicly denied involvement in the conflict, but admitted it had sent drones to Russia before the full-scale invasion of Ukraine, and Iranian officials told Reuters months into the war that Tehran had agreed to supply more drones and missiles. 

Leaked contract documents indicate that Russia agreed to pay approximately $290,000 per drone for a bulk purchase of 2,000 Shahed-136 drones, although the extent to which these payments were completed remains unclear. Iran has also reportedly helped to establish production facilities in Russia, enabling Moscow to domestically manufacture a modified version of Iran’s Shahed-136 drone named Geran-2. 

However, influential voices in Tehran have often questioned the strategic alliance with Moscow. One former IRGC naval commander said ‘There is a view that Russia sought to drag Iran into that [Ukraine] war … so it would not be alone and the pressure of sanctions would increase on Iran.’ In 2022, the US and EU imposed additional sanctions on Iran over its sales of drones to Russia. During Lavrov’s previous visit to Tehran in February 2025, Iranian commentators warned that Moscow might use Iran as a bargaining chip in negotiations with Washington over Ukraine. 

Critics of closer relations have also argued that Russia was benefiting disproportionately from Tehran’s support, without providing comparable assistance in return. In particular, Tehran felt Russia did not significantly come to its aid during the 12-day war between Iran and Israel in June 2025. Russia failed to deliver advanced weapons systems that Iran said it had purchased before the war, such as SU-35 fighter jets.

Support for closer cooperation

The US-Israeli war appears to have prompted a reassessment of Russia’s value to Tehran. According to several reports, Russia provided Iran with intelligence on US military positions, satellite imagery for targeting, and weapons components. It is difficult to assess the real battlefield impact of Russian support. However, despite President Donald Trump’s statement that Moscow and Beijing have not been helping Tehran, the evidence suggests otherwise.

Such support is likely to have strengthened the position of those within Iran’s security establishment who have long advocated closer ties with Moscow. For this group, who were supported by the late former president, Ebrahim Raisi, the war has vindicated their longstanding argument that closer cooperation with Russia could deliver tangible strategic benefits. These include helping Iran circumvent sanctions, overcoming diplomatic isolation and countering Western pressure. 

The increasingly positive statements from senior political officials such as Pezeshkian and Araghchi suggests that support for closer cooperation with Russia is becoming more widespread across the Iranian political spectrum, including among those once sceptical of close alignment with Moscow.  

As Tehran prioritizes military survival, deterrence, and reconstruction in the coming months, closer cooperation with Russia will likely be increasingly seen as a strategic necessity rather than merely as a means of circumventing sanctions and resisting Western pressure. The partnership is acquiring a more immediate security rationale, serving both Iran’s current military requirements and its longer-term strategic objectives.

Consequences

In the short term, technical assistance and weapons components could help Iran withstand the conflict by sustaining capabilities degraded by months of fighting. Russian expertise could help Tehran rebuild its air defences, missile infrastructure, and defence industry. Russian intelligence could help Iranian forces track US military assets and inform operational decisions. 

Russian support will be particularly valuable in the event of renewed military escalation. It could improve Iran’s ability to anticipate attacks, preserve its military capabilities and impose costs on its adversaries. However, it is unlikely to fundamentally alter the balance of power in Iran’s favour.

In the medium term, assuming the war comes to an end, Iran-Russia cooperation will likely continue with the aim of rebuilding Iran’s military capabilities. This would likely focus on air defence, drones and missile technology. 

While Russia’s capacity to meet Iran’s demands will remain constrained by its war in Ukraine and pressure on its defence industry, even selective transfers of technology and expertise would help Tehran address its vulnerabilities and accelerate the restoration of its deterrent capabilities. For example, Russia could provide replacement components for the S-300 missile defence system as well as electronic warfare technology.

In the longer term, the most consequential outcome could be the institutionalization of military cooperation between Iran and Russia. Iranian policymakers will remain wary of Russia’s tendency to prioritize its own interests and the absence of a binding security guarantee. But the relationship is likely to become increasingly central in future military planning, procurement and defence-industrial cooperation. This will likely increase Iran’s ability to withstand US military and economic pressure, albeit without being a game changer in the balance of power.

The war may not have transformed Russia into a reliable security guarantor for Iran, but it could make Moscow a more enduring component of Tehran’s security strategy. This will ensure the partnership is harder to reverse, no matter who is in power.

title: China has the APEC stage. But Japan may have the momentum
author: jon.wallace
description:
China has the APEC stage. But Japan may have the momentum Expert comment jon.wallace 13 November 2026

Tokyo cannot compete with Beijing’s economic firepower. But it offers Indo-Pacific countries a diplomatic and economic partner that delivers tangible gains without demanding allegiance in return.

The Asian Century is upon us with China as its visionary leader. That will be the message Beijing will hope to drive home when it hosts the Asia-Pacific Economic Cooperation (APEC) summit on 18 to 19 November.
    
The summit is billed as a forum to address ‘building an Asia-Pacific community to prosper together’. But it will take place as the world’s most populous region grapples with challenges of energy insecurity, supply chain disruption, AI governance, and technological upheaval – and as growing geopolitical tensions are causing the realignment of international partnerships. 
    
Beijing has not shied away from promoting itself as champion of the Global South. But for Indo-Pacific economies seeking a partner to build consensus and tackle the region’s most pressing challenges, the momentum may well be with Japan.

Low expectations

China’s history of lifting its people out of poverty at breathtaking speed has been nothing short of remarkable. Nevertheless, there is a trust deficit across the Indo-Pacific, where Beijing has established itself as the undisputed regional hegemon.

Its vision for growth, as outlined in in its latest Five-Year Plan, seeks to make China the global leader in advanced technology by 2030. But there are concerns among regional countries that this will mean Beijing further exploits its dominance and exacerbates global economic warfare.

Meanwhile expectations for gatherings such as APEC, and the ASEAN summit in the Philippines preceding it, are low. The possibility of a display of unity, let alone a collective action plan, seems remote, especially as China will continue to leverage its chokeholds on the global economy. Instead, more attention will be paid to meetings on the sidelines of the summits, including a likely trilateral between Presidents Donald Trump, Xi Jinping, and Vladimir Putin. 

Those talks are expected to focus on the Iran war and denuclearization. A breakthrough on the war would be greatly welcomed, given the economic pain caused by the resulting higher energy costs: Southeast and South Asian countries including Vietnam have been hard hit. But the underlying concern for regional countries will be that shifting relations between the US, China and Russia could further aggravate their existing challenges.

China will remain an indispensable relationship for all countries in the region. But it is Japan that may hold the key to a collaborative path to address the Indo-Pacific’s challenges – one that might allow the region to continue its upward economic trajectory.

An evolving strategy

There are three main reasons that Japan could play a key role as a driver of collaboration in the region. 
    
First, Tokyo’s Free and Open Indo-Pacific (FOIP) strategy has evolved to meet the new strategic reality. Originally FOIP championed a rules-based order, quickly becoming the foundation for the Indo-Pacific strategies of governments including the US and European Union. Its weakness, though, was the reluctance of South and Southeast Asian nations to embrace it. That, and the geopolitical reality of weakening commitment to a rules-based international order.      
    
Tokyo has responded by developing the strategy around a pragmatic, results-oriented approach. In her May 2026 speech before the Vietnam National University, Japanese Prime Minister Sanae Takaichi again stressed the need for a rules-based economic order. But she also set out how Japan intends to update the FOIP to reflect the immediate, practical needs of Vietnam and other countries across the Indo-Pacific.

That includes initiatives to build economic infrastructure ‘for the age of AI’, such as underwater sea cables and satellite communications, creating a ‘FOIP digital corridor’. It also means enhancing energy security for the long term, as outlined by the $10 billion Partnership on Wide Energy and Resource Resilience Asia (POWERR Asia), which Tokyo is expanding as it collaborates with the World Bank to advance regional energy resilience.

And it means boosting regional cooperation on artificial intelligence through an ASEAN-Japan Co-Creation Initiative for AI.

A trusted partner

Second, Japan has emerged as one of the most trusted and politically stable countries in the Indo-Pacific. In the latest State of Southeast Asia survey, Japan is ranked the most trusted major power by respondents in the 10 ASEAN nations for the eighth consecutive year. Nearly 66 per cent of respondents regard Japan as a responsible stakeholder that would do the right thing for global peace and prosperity. That puts it in a position to operate as a regional consensus-builder that can bring forward a roadmap for regional growth.

Granted, Tokyo has no interest in becoming a ‘superpower of the middle powers’. But it continues to embrace taking on a greater role in an increasingly unstable region that is facing growing economic risks. And it has shown an ability to overcome significant tensions and focus on results, for instance through its improved relations with Seoul – where pragmatism has generally prevailed as both Japan and South Korea have sought to cooperate over economic concerns, the increasing unpredictability of US policy, and shared regional security threats like North Korea.

Third, Japan has been committed to ensuring continued US engagement in the Indo-Pacific, including on trade. There has been growing discontent in the region about the economic damage caused by US foreign policy decisions, from tariffs to the war with Iran. But Tokyo has been resolute in promoting frameworks that would encourage the US to regain its position as a trusted economic power once again. 
    
Granted, the likelihood of the US joining a multilateral trade framework such as the CPTPP is highly unlikely, even after a new Congress is sworn in under Democratic control. But the US remains the only country that has the advanced technology and financial capital to compete head-on with China. And Washington will remain a critical partner for economic security in the Indo-Pacific moving forward.

Japan cannot single-handedly reconcile the Indo-Pacific’s divergent interests, and there is domestic political debate about to what extent Japan should take on a leadership role, given its own fiscal constraints. It clearly cannot match China’s economic heft nor the technological and financial firepower of the US. Moreover, the trust that it enjoys in Southeast Asia does not necessarily translate into becoming a leader. Yet that may be to its advantage as the Indo-Pacific navigates the shifting global order and adopting to new geopolitical realities.

What Tokyo offers is a partner that delivers tangible results without demanding allegiance in return. Japan is positioning itself not as a regional leader, but as the convener the Indo-Pacific increasingly needs.

This column examines how transportation bottlenecks interact with aggregate shocks, comparing the Commodity Supercycle of the 2000s and the post-pandemic Great Supply Chain Disruption. The spike in freight rates for dry bulk shipping in the former episode was due to scarce shipping capacity, while the latter stemmed from scarce port capacity. Shipping prices rise dramatically when transportation capacity is scarce, while port prices remain much more stable. The constraint matters: when ships are scarce, shipowners have strong incentives to order new vessels, but addressing port scarcity may require government intervention.

description:

And the discovery of the PHP flaw that sent websites offline in October came from researchers working with AI, not from a bounty hunter's report.

Tobias Kretschmer (Imperial College London, CEPR) and his co-authors followed 86 programmes on Bugcrowd to discover how they work best. title: Labour market origins of experimentation and growth: Why Europe is falling behind
author: Renato Faccini, Seho Kim, Javier Miranda
description: Europe’s innovation gap with the US and China lies in breakthrough rather than incremental innovation. This column argues that part of the explanation is the labour market. Breakthroughs come from risky experimentation and experiments often fail and cost workers their jobs. When job loss is costly, workers demand a wage premium to join risky young firms, and that premium acts as a tax on experimentation. Combining a new model, Danish matched employer–employee data and a randomised survey experiment, the authors show that more fluid labour markets lower this premium, raise experimentation, and lift aggregate productivity.

Combining data on populist leaders with surveys of more than 260,000 people in 53 countries, it shows that people exposed to populist governments during early adulthood develop more zero-sum views for around two decades. This is more consistent with a rhetorical channel than with an explanation based on economic hardship.
